title: Adaptive Conformal Anomaly Detection with Time Series Foundation Models
one_liner: Wrap pretrained time series models with an adaptive confidence layer that gives honest false alarm rates and learns from new data without retraining.
lead: Time series sensors (factory equipment, network traffic, patient monitors) need anomaly detection, but real sensors drift. Most methods either require huge labeled datasets to train, or give opaque scores you cannot trust. This paper adds a thin adaptive layer on top of any pretrained time series model: it yields an interpretable false alarm rate (called a p-value) and learns to adapt as the normal signal drifts, without retraining the underlying model.

problem.h2: Why existing methods break with drifting sensors
paras: A pretrained time series model (trained on millions of past signals) can predict the next sensor value well, even if you have no data from your specific factory. But real signals drift over time: today's normal equipment hum is not tomorrow's normal equipment hum. If you ask the model to guess the next value and compare it to reality, the error sizes change.

A naive approach: pick a fixed threshold on the error (e.g., if the model's guess is off by more than 5 units, raise an alarm). This breaks immediately. When the signal drifts to a new quiet state, errors shrink, and the threshold fires false alarms. When the signal drifts to a new noisier state, errors grow, and you miss real anomalies. You need a threshold that moves with the signal.

Even worse: a bare prediction error gives you a raw number, not a false alarm rate. Is an error of 3 units dangerous or normal? You never know. You want the system to say: given what we see, the false alarm rate is 2% if we raise an alarm right now.

callout.html: Layer an adaptive conformal predictor on top of a pretrained model: it gives you a false alarm rate for each decision and tunes itself as the signal drifts, using only the errors it sees, no retraining.

steps.text: Feed the last few sensor readings in; predict the next reading.
Take the real reading; compute how far the guess was.
Assign each past error a weight: recent errors count more, old errors count less.
Find the threshold (quantile) of weighted errors above which lies the alarm zone.

steps.b: Report an honest false alarm rate
steps.text: Say: if we alarm now, our false alarm rate is this fraction (a p-value).

paras: It does not change the pretrained model. It adds a thin layer on top that learns weights for past prediction errors. These weights steer how high the alarm threshold climbs, adapting it to the signal's current noise level without any retraining.

hidden.name: p-value: the expected false alarm rate
paras: A p-value (here called a false alarm rate or false alarm probability) is a number between 0 and 1 that says: if we raise an alarm right now based on this data, what fraction of our future alarms will be lies? A p-value of 0.02 means 2% false alarms; 0.05 means 5%. It is not a probability that this specific point is an anomaly; it is a rate across many future decisions.

The paper estimates the p-value by looking at past forecast errors. It sorts the errors by age, weights recent ones more, and finds the point where (roughly) 1 in 100 errors exceeds the threshold if the false alarm target is 1%. This number adapts every time a new error arrives.

heat.caption: Hot cells (red): recent errors and their high weights. Threshold (darker) moves as weights shift.

reads.html: A p-value tells you the false alarm rate: if you alarm every time a sensor error exceeds this threshold, roughly this fraction will be false alarms.

The method computes a weighted quantile of past prediction errors: a conformal bound that grows or shrinks with signal drift, yielding a guarantee that holds regardless of how the noise pattern changes.

mechanism.h2: Why weighted quantiles adapt without retraining
paras: The core insight: forecast errors tell you everything. When the signal shifts to a noisier state, all the prediction errors grow together; when it shifts quieter, they shrink. You do not need to retrain the model because the model is already good at predicting the signal (it was trained on millions of examples). You only need to tune your alarm threshold to match the current noise level.

The paper learns weights for each past error. Recent errors get high weight because they reflect the signal's current state; older errors get low weight because the signal has likely drifted. It then finds the quantile (threshold) such that if you alarm whenever an error crosses it, your false alarm rate hits your target (e.g., 5%). As new errors stream in, the weights shift, the quantile moves, and the alarm threshold adapts without touching the model.

Why does this work? Because the weights are chosen to make the false alarm rate true at every horizon (1-step-ahead, 2-steps-ahead, etc.). The weighted quantile is a conformal prediction technique: it gives a provable finite-sample guarantee. Even with distribution shift (signal drift), even with no labeled anomalies, the false alarm rate is guaranteed to hold.

stages.s: Pretrained model + stream of new sensor errors
Collect errors into a rolling history, newest at the end
Assign weights: recent errors high, old errors low
Sort weighted errors; find the threshold that gives your target false alarm rate
When a new error arrives, update weights and threshold
Anomaly score (p-value) and alarm decision per sample

math.words: Weighted quantile threshold equals the error level below which lies a fraction of the weighted errors, chosen so the false alarm rate (alpha) is met. New weights minimize prediction error variance across past observations, adjusted for each prediction horizon.
math.equation: Threshold_alpha = quantile_alpha( weighted_errors ), where weights_d = argmin_w sum_t w_t * error_d,t^2 subject to sum_t w_t = 1, and p-value = 1 - Phi( (error_t - Threshold) / std )
symbols: the alarm level for false alarm rate alpha (e.g., alpha=0.05 for 5% FAR)
the weighted quantile function: find the error level where alpha fraction of weighted errors lie below
past prediction errors, each multiplied by its learned weight
learned weights for each past error at horizon d, summing to 1
prediction error at time t for d-step-ahead forecast
false alarm rate reported to the user (between 0 and 1)
the cumulative standard normal function (converts a z-score to a probability)

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Assign weights: oldest errors (indices 0-9) each get weight 0.01; newest (10-19) each get weight 0.05. Total: 10 * 0.01 + 10 * 0.05 = 0.6, normalize to 1.0.
Compute cumulative weighted sum: at error=0.5, cumulative weight = 0.30. At error=0.6, cumulative = 0.50. At error=0.7, cumulative = 0.65.
For 95th percentile (alpha=0.05), find where cumulative weight crosses 0.95: around error=0.85. Threshold_0.05 = 0.85.
Today you observe a new error: 0.72. Since 0.72 < 0.85, no alarm. Report p-value = 0.10 (this error lies in the 10th percentile of weighted history).

math.note: The weights tilt the quantile toward recent errors, so the threshold climbs or falls with the signal's current noise. Conformal prediction guarantees that the p-values (false alarm rates) remain honest even as the signal drifts.

charts.title: Naive: fixed threshold on raw error
charts.note: False alarm rate swings wildly: 8% when quiet, 66% when noisy, 12% when quiet again. Threshold does not adapt.

charts.title: This paper (W1-ACAS): adaptive conformal
charts.note: False alarm rate stays near 5% across all drifts. Weights move the threshold automatically, no model retraining needed.

items.b: Too little history at the start.
items.html: When you first deploy the system, you have only a handful of past errors. The quantile is unreliable. Solution: collect a small clean dataset at deployment (a few hours of sensor data without anomalies) to seed the weight table.

items.b: Sudden, permanent shift in the true normal signal.
items.html: If the equipment breaks and stays broken (a new normal that is not an anomaly but a mode change), the weights will eventually learn the new normal and stop alarming. This is correct behavior, but it means you need external input to label mode changes versus true anomalies.

items.b: Anomaly that looks like a very large error.
items.html: If an anomaly is extreme enough, the prediction error grows so large that the quantile method will take a long time to shift above it. The method is conservative (low false alarm rate), so it may miss the very first occurrence of a new anomaly type.

Use a pretrained model on your domain (time series foundation models work well). Collect a few hours of clean data at start. Monitor the false alarm rate (it should stay near your alpha target). If it drifts noticeably over weeks (alarm rate climbs to 10% or drops to 1%), retrain the weights table or add fresh clean data.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a simple time series: a sine wave (normal behavior) with occasional spikes (anomalies). Use a pretrained foundation model (or train a tiny LSTM on just the sine part) to predict the next value. Then run the algorithm: collect errors, learn weights, compute thresholds, and raise alarms. Plot (1) the signal, (2) the model's predictions, (3) the prediction errors over time, (4) the learned weights (showing recency bias), and (5) the p-values (false alarm rates). The key is to show that when the signal's noise level changes, the threshold adapts and the p-values stay near your target (e.g., 5%) without retraining the model.
demo.metric_eq: False Alarm Rate = (# alarms on clean signal) / (# total samples in clean period). True detection rate = (# alarms on real anomalies) / (# real anomalies). Desired behavior: FAR stays near alpha (5%), detection rises with anomaly magnitude.
demo.closing: The demo must show the weighted threshold moving in lockstep with signal noise, and the reported false alarm rate (p-value) staying stable as the signal drifts.
